work.author: Richard Jefferies
work.title: Bevis: The Story of a Boy

preamble: Bevis and Mark are two boys exploring the shore of a lake near their home, which they are treating as a voyage of discovery. Bevis has appointed himself captain of the expedition and Mark his lieutenant. Pan is Bevis’s dog. They have been lying still at the water’s edge, watching two great fish move slowly along the bottom.
extract:
“Go and fetch my fishing-rod,” whispered Bevis, unable to speak loud; he was so excited.

“No, you go,” said Mark; “I’ll stay and watch them.”

“I shan’t,” said Bevis sharply, “you ought to go.”

“I shan’t,” said Mark.

Just then the tench, having surveyed the bottom there, turned and faded away into the darker deep water.

“There,” said Bevis, “if you had run quick!”

“I won’t fetch everything,” said Mark.

“Then you’re no use,” said Bevis. “Suppose I was shooting an elephant, and you did not hand me another gun quick, or another arrow; and suppose--”

“But _I_ might be shooting the elephant,” interrupted Mark, “and you could hand me the gun.”

“Impossible,” said Bevis; “I never heard anything so absurd. Of course it’s the captain who always does everything; and if there was only one biscuit left, of course you would let me eat it, and lie down and die under a tree, so that I might go on and reach the settlement.”

“I _hate_ dying under a tree,” said Mark, “and you always want everything.”

Bevis said nothing, but marched on very upright and very angry, and Mark followed, putting his feet into the marks Bevis left as he strode over the yielding sand. Neither spoke a word. The shore trended in again after the point, and the indentation was full of weeds, whose broad brownish leaves floated on the surface. Pan worked about and sniffed among the willow bushes on their left, which, when the lake was full, were in the water, but now that it had shrunk under the summer heat were several yards from the edge.

Bevis, leading the way, came to a place where the strand, till then so low and shelving, suddenly became steep, where a slight rise of the ground was cut as it were through by the water, which had worn a cliff eight or ten feet above his head. The water came to the bottom of the cliff, and there did not seem any way past it except by going away from the edge into the field, and so round it. Mark at once went round, hastening as fast as he could to get in front, and he came down to the water on the other side of the cliff in half a minute, looked at Bevis, and then went on with Pan.

Bevis, with a frown on his forehead, stood looking at the cliff, having determined that he would not go round, and yet he could not get past because the water, which was dark and deep, going straight down, came to the bank, which rose from it like a wall. First he took out his pocket-knife and thought he would cut steps in the sand, and he did cut one large enough to put his toe in; but then he recollected that he should have nothing to hold to. He had half a mind to go back home and get some big nails and drive into the hard sand to catch hold of, only by that time Mark would be so far ahead he could not overtake him and would boast that he had explored the new sea first. Already he was fifty yards in front, and walking as fast as he could. How he wished he had his raft, and then that he could swim! He would have jumped into the water and swam round the cliff in a minute.

He saw Mark climbing over some railings that went down to the water to divide the fields. He looked up again at the cliff, and almost felt inclined to leave it and run round and overtake Mark. When he looked down again Mark was out of sight, hidden by hawthorn bushes and the branches of trees. Bevis was exceedingly angry, and he walked up and down and gazed round in his rage. But as he turned once more to the cliff, suddenly Pan appeared at an opening in the furze and bramble about halfway up. The bushes grew at the side, and the spaniel, finding Bevis did not follow Mark, had come back and was waiting for him. Bevis, without thinking, pushed into the furze, and immediately he saw him coming, Pan, eager to go forward again, ran along the face of the cliff about four feet from the top. He seemed to run on nothing, and Bevis was curious to see how he had got by.

The bushes becoming thicker, Bevis had at last to go on hands and knees under them, and found a hollow space, where there was a great rabbit-bury, big enough at the mouth for Pan to creep in. When he stood on the sand thrown out from it he could see how Pan had done it; there was a narrow ledge, not above four inches wide, on the face of the cliff. It was only just wide enough for a footing, and the cliff fell sheer down to the water; but Bevis, seeing that he could touch the top of the cliff, and so steady himself, never hesitated a moment.

He stepped on the ledge, right foot first, the other close behind it, and hold lightly to the grass at the edge of the field above, only lightly lest he should pull it out by the roots. Then he put his right foot forward again, and drew his left up to it, and so along, keeping the right first (he could not walk properly, the ledge being so narrow), he worked himself along. It was quite easy, though it seemed a long way down to the water, it always looks very much farther down than it does up, and as he glanced down he saw a perch rise from the depths, and it occurred to him in the moment what a capital place it would be for perch-fishing.

He could see all over that part of the lake, and noticed two moorhens feeding in the weeds on the other side, when puff! the wind came over the field, and reminded him, as he involuntarily grasped the grass tighter, that he must not stay in such a place where he might lose his balance. So he went on, and a dragonfly flew past out a little way over the water and then back to the field, but Bevis was not to be tempted to watch his antics, he kept steadily on, a foot at a time, till he reached a willow on the other side, and had a bough to hold. Then he shouted, and Pan, who was already far ahead, stopped and looked back at the well-known sound of triumph.

Running down the easy slope, Bevis quickly reached the railings and climbed over. On the other side a meadow came down to the edge, and he raced through the grass and was already halfway to the next rails when some one called “Bevis!” and there was Mark coming out from behind an oak in the field. Bevis stopped, half-pleased, half-angry.

“I waited for you,” said Mark.

“I came across the cliff,” said Bevis.

“I saw you,” said Mark.

“But you ran away from me,” said Bevis.

“But I am not running now.”

“It is very wrong when we are on an expedition,” said Bevis. “People must do as the captain tells them.”

“I won’t do it again,” said Mark.

“You ought to be punished,” said Bevis, “you ought to be put on half-rations. Are you quite sure you will never do it again?”

“Never.”

“Well then, this once you are pardoned. Now, mind in future, as you are lieutenant, you set a good example. There’s a summer snipe.”

curationNotes: Chosen over the raft-building and the sinking, which is the novel’s best-known sequence and is 3,000 words of practical detail with no complication in it. Chosen over the tench-watching immediately before this, which is beautiful and static. This is the only compact stretch in the first volume where something is at stake between the two boys and is settled. BAND: 1,277 words, over the CSSE ceiling by 177 — see bandException.

bandException.status: RESTATED 2026-08-14 against the short band — 327 over, not 177
bandException.correctionNotice: A previous report put this at ~1,170 words and 6%. That was my arithmetic error. Re-confirmed on the true figure, on the ground that the argument was never about the size of the excess.

whyNotTrimmed.verdict: Dropping the cliff traverse reaches 908 words and makes the extract CONTRADICT itself: four paragraphs later Bevis says "I came across the cliff", which he then never does. That is worse than a seam — it is a false statement inside the passage.

whyNotTrimmed.route: drop the two paragraphs before the traverse
whyNotTrimmed.verdict: Dropping the two paragraphs before the traverse reaches 930 words and breaks two antecedents at once: "The bushes becoming thicker" with no bushes introduced, and "reached the railings" with no railings introduced.
Dropping the whole traverse reaches 439 words, far under any band, and removes the reason the two boys are apart when they meet again.
whyNotTrimmed.whyItIsRecordedAnyway: AT 439 WORDS THIS WAS NEVER AN IN-BAND ALTERNATIVE and the original prose says so — "far under any band". It is recorded for a different purpose from the other two: they are selections a curator was ALLOWED to make and which break the extract, which is what the no-shorter-selection ground rests on. This one demonstrates that the traverse cannot simply be removed wholesale. Flagged when the standing alternatives check fired on it, because the structure had been treating all three as the same kind of evidence. THE GROUND RESTS ON TWO ALTERNATIVES, NOT THREE.

bandException.whatContiguityBuys: Twenty-nine paragraphs with no internal cut cannot carry a seam or a broken antecedent, because both faults are created by cutting. This is the first extract in the bank where the authoring read had nothing to find, and the reason is structural.
bandException.restatementNotice: The excess was declared against CSSE, the more forgiving of two readings, and was 177. Against the band the record actually puts this passage in, the same 1,277 words are 327 over, 34.4%. NOTHING IN THE ARGUMENT CHANGES. The three built alternatives were re-measured under the declared word measure and reproduce exactly — 908, 930, 439 — and the first two are still INSIDE the short band, so they remain genuine in-band alternatives rejected on sense rather than on arithmetic. If anything the ground is stronger: the short ceiling demands dropping 327 words rather than 177, so fewer selections reach it at all.

enumeration.method: Every removal of one to four paragraphs from the twenty-nine, measured under words-alnum-runs-v1.
enumeration.finding: EVERY route to 950 cuts into paragraphs 12-18, the cliff traverse. That is the block all three recorded alternatives break, and it is the block that carries "I came across the cliff" four paragraphs later, the bushes that thicken, and the railings Bevis reaches. There is no selection at 950 that leaves it alone.
enumeration.andTheItemTestIsUnavailable: Bevis carries no cluster yet, so unlike Christmas Carol there are no live items to test a route against. The test here is the recorded self-contradiction and the two broken antecedents, which is a weaker instrument and is named as one.

bandException.alternativesAreRecomputable: Each rejected alternative carries the paragraphs it drops, so the figure is re-derived from the extract rather than trusted. This exists because an exception resting on "no shorter selection survives" depends on those alternatives being IN band, and a ceiling or measure change can push them out without the exception looking any different on the page.
bandException.groundRestsOn: Two in-band alternatives, 908 and 930, both inside the short band and both breaking the extract — a self-contradiction and two broken antecedents. The third recorded route is out of band by design and is evidence for a different claim.

complicationSeparation.description: Bevis’s claim about captains, made to win an argument he is losing, against the same claim made to close one he has won.

complicationSeparation.halfBAnchor: People must do as the captain tells them
complicationSeparation.sceneBeatBetween: the angry march, the cliff, and the meeting at the railings
complicationSeparation.descriptionIsAKnownHook: KEPT DELIBERATELY, RULED 2026-08-14. This field STATES THE RELATION and therefore hands a drafter the T4 key. That is a fault by the test the Stream-B anchors were built to pass — learn where to look, not what the answer is — and it is NOT being repaired. Removing it would destroy a baseline and change retrospectively what four already-built clusters mean. The divergence is recorded as a controlled comparison instead: see complication_find_rate.py, arm 1. Any NEW Stream-A passage should carry anchors without a description.

narratorialSignposting.closest: Bevis said nothing, but marched on very upright and very angry
narratorialSignposting.reading: Feelings are named in this extract — angry, a frown — so the passage is not withholding inner states. What it withholds is any verdict on the game: Bevis asserts the rules of an expedition he invented as though they were facts, four times, and the narrator neither endorses nor mocks a single one of them. That silence is never remarked on.

authoringRead.openingReference: FAULT FOUND IN THE PASSAGE THAT WAS SUPPOSED TO HAVE NOTHING TO FIND, AND FIXED IN THE PREAMBLE. Bevis is the extract cited in Addendum 28 as proof that a contiguous selection cannot carry a reference fault. Its second paragraph is Mark saying "No, you go; I’ll stay and watch THEM" — and the fish are not introduced until four paragraphs later, at "Just then the tench...". The front trim dropped the tench-watching, and with it every antecedent the opening exchange leans on. Twenty-nine contiguous paragraphs, zero internal cuts, one broken reference: the seam claim in Addendum 28 stands, the antecedent claim does not. The preamble now carries the two great fish. Otherwise clean: Bevis is named in the first sentence and Mark in the second, and no other opening reference points outside the extract.
